strengths: Novel integration of classical psychophysics with modern vision transformers through large-scale behavioral experiment (1020 trials, 72 participants) with rigorous methodology including eye-tracking and fixation validation
Comprehensive model evaluation across architectures and training objectives clearly demonstrates training objective matters more than architecture for object-centricity
ROC-based metric for quantifying object-centric structure in patch representations is principled, doesn't require supervision, and generalizable across models
Strong empirical finding of tight correlation between object-centric AUC and behavioral alignment (Fig. 6B) across all model types, suggesting fundamental organizing principle

Gram matrix alignment findings are mechanistically informative and novel, showing supervised models can be improved by matching self-supervised feature correlation structure; convergence with independent DINOv3 design choices strengthens evidence
Consistent improvements from Gram alignment across all four tested models (8-18% gains), with Transformer models showing larger improvements than ConvNets
Clear presentation with informative visualizations; well-designed figures effectively communicate results
Behavioral patterns (same-object advantage, distance effects) appropriately validate task and replicate prior findings
weaknesses: Limited scope of behavioral dataset: only 255 images after filtering from 288 candidates, biased toward images with overlapping objects, all from COCO dataset, potentially reducing generalizability to natural image distribution

Significant gap between best model (~0.75 normalized correlation) and human performance not adequately explained; no systematic analysis of failure modes or scene properties that challenge models despite mentioning specific factors (within-object boundaries, texture differences)

Gram matrix distillation procedure underspecified: loss function not explicitly stated, weighting between classification and Gram components not provided, optimization details (learning rate, schedule, duration) missing, hyperparameter selection process unclear—reproducibility concerns

Limited mechanistic insight into why DINO learns object-centric structure: paper demonstrates THAT it does but not deeply WHY; self-distillation vs. supervised objective comparison lacks investigation of underlying mechanisms; Gram analysis is correlational

Incomplete behavioral analysis: only aggregate effects presented in Section 3.2; mentioned factors affecting RT (within-object boundaries, texture, narrowness, proximity to boundaries, category presence) not quantified; Fig. 3 only shows illustrative examples without systematic breakdown

Technical reproducibility gaps: MLP readout architecture choices not justified (why 2-layer?), no ablation on architecture; hyperparameter selection process for readout not described; sensitivity to choices not analyzed; cross-validation procedure could include more details
No statistical testing or confidence intervals provided for many model comparisons; while noise ceiling estimation is thoughtful, other comparisons lack rigor

Limited novelty: object-centric properties of DINO models already known from extensive prior literature; main contribution is behavioral validation and Gram finding; ROC metric while useful is relatively straightforward

ROC metric limitations not discussed: handling of boundary pixels unclear, sensitivity to object size not analyzed, potential background dominance bias not addressed, no comparison to alternative metrics

Missing ablations and sensitivity analyses: no justification for Gram matrices vs. other similarity measures, layer-wise analysis only for one model, only 2-layer MLP tested for readout, no ablation on DINO loss components

strengths: Rigorous and well-designed behavioral experiment scaling psychophysics paradigm to 1020 trials across natural scenes with careful experimental controls (eye tracking, counterbalancing, distance matching)—sets strong foundation for model comparison
Novel large-scale behavioral benchmark that could become valuable community resource for evaluating vision models on perceptual alignment; comprehensive documentation aids reproducibility

Comprehensive model comparison across architectures (ViT, ConvNet), training objectives (supervised, DINO variants, MAE), and scales with clear finding that training objective dominates—provides actionable insights for model design

Strong mechanistic insight into role of Gram matrix: correlation between object-centric AUC and behavioral alignment (r=0.950) is compelling, and Gram alignment experiments with proper CLS token ablation demonstrate causality (8-18 pp improvements)

Novel ROC-based object-centricity metric that quantifies patch-level object structure without requiring per-patch annotations; analysis across layers and heads provides valuable mechanistic understanding

Excellent transparency and reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, extensive supplementary material, multiple baselines (linear readout, CLS distillation), ablations confirming no side effects on classification accuracy
Convergence with independent DINOv3 findings on Gram anchoring strengthens mechanistic claims and suggests findings extend beyond this specific task
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (especially Figures 1, 5, 6) and logical flow from behavioral phenomena to mechanistic insights
weaknesses: Single behavioral task (two-dot grouping) provides narrow scope; does not test other critical aspects of object perception including figure-ground segregation, occlusion handling, part-whole hierarchies, or boundary detection in cluttered scenes—generalizability to segmentation, detection, or scene understanding uncertain

Weak behavioral signal: noise ceiling only 0.42 (raw correlations ~0.30-0.35), meaning normalized scores inflated by low ceiling; single-trial AUC much lower (0.55 vs 0.71), indicating high noise; best model (normalized r=0.83) leaves substantial unexplained variance and unclear whether models capture genuine perceptual phenomena or correlate with noisy RT variation

Architecture and training objective not fully decoupled: small sample of models per condition (3 DINO variants, 2-3 per training objective), different models trained on different datasets with different computational budgets—DINOv3 uses larger datasets than supervised baselines; factorial design would strengthen claims

Statistical concerns: correlation r=0.950 based on only 9 models (fragile to individual model), no confidence intervals or significance tests comparing adjacent models (DINOv3 vs DINOv2?), normalized correlation procedure could mask sensitivity—main results need uncertainty quantification

Limited error analysis: no investigation of model failure cases, what trial types DINOv3 gets wrong, or why supervised models fail uniformly—deeper analysis would provide richer mechanistic understanding

Gram alignment design choices under-justified: loss weight (10×) appears empirically tuned rather than principled, ConvNet models show smaller gains than Transformers despite similar setup (unexplained), theoretical explanation for why Gram structure drives object-centricity underdeveloped

Generalization and robustness concerns: all evaluation on COCO2017 (same distribution), no testing on out-of-distribution images, different object types/sizes/clutter levels, or other benchmarks; sample images suggest well-defined objects—unclear how findings extend to ambiguous/cluttered/overlapping scenarios

Missing comparisons: no evaluation of simpler baselines (texture, edge-based models), no comparison to other computational models of human vision, no comparison to human object recognition accuracy on same images or recent foundation models

Object-centric metric limitations: requires ground truth object annotations (cannot compute on fully unsupervised), sensitivity to annotation quality unexplored, only measures similarity structure (not texture, edges, etc.), generalization to ambiguous boundaries unclear

Limited novelty in findings: DINO models' object-centric properties already documented in prior work (LOST, TokenCut, visual anagrams); gap to human performance (normalized r<1.0) shows models substantially incomplete; unclear whether findings impact real applications beyond controlled lab task

strengths: Rigorous behavioral benchmark with high-quality data (90% accuracy, 2.78 d-prime across 72 subjects, 1020 trials) and careful experimental design including eye-tracking validation and counterbalancing
Novel unsupervised object-centricity metric based on ROC analysis that quantifies object-centric structure without requiring object-level supervision
Strong empirical finding: object-centric AUC correlates robustly with behavioral alignment (r=0.950, p=0.0001) across diverse models, suggesting a general principle
Comprehensive evaluation spanning 9 models with different architectures (ViT, ConvNext) and training objectives (supervised, DINO variants, MAE)
Methodologically sound with proper nested cross-validation, human noise ceiling normalization, control baselines (linear readout, CLS distillation), and extensive supplementary materials
Gram matrix alignment experiments provide mechanistic insight into one factor (patch feature correlation) that drives object-centric representations
weaknesses: Limited novelty of core claims: that DINO models capture object-centric structure is already documented in prior work; main contribution is behavioral grounding, which is somewhat incremental

Substantial 17% gap between best model and human noise ceiling (83% normalized correlation) remains poorly explained—no systematic analysis of failure modes, when/why models diverge, or whether gap is fundamental

Shallow mechanistic insight into Gram alignment: why does feature correlation structure matter for binding? Connection to classical association field theory unclear; feels post-hoc rather than predictive
Architecture and training objective not properly decoupled despite acknowledged confounding; no controlled experiments isolate their relative contributions to alignment

Limited scope and generalization: only 255 images, single experimental paradigm (two-dot task), no evaluation on other grouping tasks (segmentation, parts, occlusion); unclear if findings generalize beyond this specific setup
Naive readout design (simple MLP on concatenated features) ignores spatial relationships, attention patterns, layer depth; more sophisticated readouts untested and could better predict behavior
Behavioral noise ceiling is surprisingly low (0.42 Spearman r); insufficient analysis of whether this reflects trial variability, subject variability, or task ambiguity
Missing systematic analysis of failure cases, error patterns, and model-human divergence; Figure 3 shows anecdotal examples only
Hyperparameter choices for Gram distillation appear arbitrary (loss weight 10:1 ratio, fine-tuning only last block); no sensitivity analysis provided
Limited practical impact: findings don't translate to novel design principles beyond using self-supervised learning and attending to Gram structure—both already embedded in modern models like DINOv3

strengths: Large-scale, well-controlled behavioral experiment (72 subjects, 1020 trials) with rigorous experimental design including eye-tracking, proper counterbalancing, and matched spatial distances to prevent confounding

Comprehensive model evaluation across 9 diverse models spanning different architectures (Transformer/ConvNet) and training regimes (self-supervised/supervised/masked autoencoding), with proper nested cross-validation and human noise ceiling normalization

Novel unsupervised metric for object-centricity based on ROC analysis that quantifies object-centric structure without object-level supervision and shows strong correlation with behavioral alignment (r=0.950, p<0.0001)

Clear and consistent empirical findings across multiple metrics demonstrating that self-supervised DINO models achieve superior alignment with human object perception compared to supervised counterparts, with training objective mattering more than architecture

Mechanistic insights from Gram matrix experiments showing that transferring patch-level correlation structure from DINOv3 to supervised models yields 8-18 percentage point improvements, with proper ablations (CLS token baseline) isolating patch-level correlation as the active ingredient

Excellent reproducibility with detailed supplementary material, implementation details, hyperparameters, and multiple validation approaches (linear readout baseline, layer-wise analysis, condition-split correlations)
Well-written and clearly presented with effective visualizations of affinity maps, ROC curves, and behavioral patterns that clearly support the narrative
weaknesses: Limited theoretical depth: while the paper demonstrates that Gram structure predicts behavioral alignment, it does not explain *why* patch-level similarity correlates with human grouping behavior; the connection to classical theories of association fields remains underdeveloped

Behavioral task limitations: the two-dot judgment paradigm is somewhat artificial compared to natural vision, constrained to configurations with one dot on central object and one on periphery, and uses RT as an indirect proxy for grouping difficulty rather than direct segmentation measures

Narrow model scope: evaluation limited to Base-sized models (ViT-B, ConvNext-B); unclear whether findings generalize to larger models (ViT-L, ViT-H) where scaling effects might differ; recent vision models missing

Substantial gap between best model and noise ceiling (0.83 normalized correlation vs. 1.0): significant room for unknown factors remains, and single-trial RT prediction is highly noisy (AUC=0.55-0.59), limiting per-trial predictability

Limited analysis of failure modes and visual factors: paper does not systematically characterize when/why models mispredict, and mentions but does not quantify how visual properties (within-object boundaries, texture differences, narrow parts) affect difficulty

Gram alignment experiments lack full characterization: only 4 models tested for alignment, only last-block fine-tuning explored, and the Gram loss weight (10×) appears arbitrary with no ablation provided; limited baselines beyond CLS distillation

Generalization concerns: unclear whether findings extend to multi-object scenes, out-of-distribution images, dynamic scenes, or other object grouping tasks; COCO dataset annotation quality and biases not discussed

Missing mechanistic depth: insufficient exploration of why Transformers respond better to Gram alignment than ConvNets; no analysis of whether self-attention patterns directly correlate with human eye gaze or grouping difficulty
